Could One Photo Change How You See Earth?

Episode 44 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌍
On Christmas Eve 1968, Apollo 8's three astronauts became the first humans to orbit the Moon, and Bill Anders took Earthrise, the photo of our planet rising over the lunar horizon. The story behind it, 58 years ago tonight.

segments.text: Could a single photo change how you see your whole planet? One did, on Christmas Eve.
On December twenty-first, nineteen sixty-eight, three astronauts launched on Apollo eight: Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders.
segments.headline: Apollo 8

segments.text: They would be the first humans ever to leave Earth's orbit and travel to the Moon.
On Christmas Eve, they reached the Moon and circled it ten times. They saw the far side with their own eyes. No human had ever seen it before.
segments.headline: Around the Moon

segments.text: On the fourth orbit, Earth came up over the lunar horizon. Anders grabbed a camera. You're looking at the photo he took: Earthrise.
segments.headline: Earthrise

segments.text: Our entire world: every person, every ocean, every border, in one small blue ball.
That night they read from the Book of Genesis in a live broadcast. It became one of the most watched television broadcasts in history.
segments.headline: A Christmas Eve broadcast

segments.text: Many people say Earthrise helped start the modern environmental movement. From space, Earth looked beautiful, and fragile.
segments.headline: A fragile home

segments.text: That was fifty-eight years ago tonight. Merry Christmas, from Next Stop Universe.
Tomorrow, visitors from other stars, flying right through our solar system. Next stop: interstellar visitors. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
